title: Magnetic Tweezers for the Measurement of Twist and Torque
protocol: Prepare DNA constructs ligated to duplex ends with biotin and digoxigenin groups.
Use a DNA tether length greater than 1 µm, such as a 7.9 kbp fragment.
Assemble flow cells for single-molecule experiments using two glass microscope coverslips separated by a double-layer Parafilm spacer.
Drill holes in the top microscope coverslip for fluid in- and outlets using a sandblaster.
Coat the bottom coverslip with nitrocellulose at 0.1% wt/vol in amyl acetate.
Place Parafilm spacers on the nitrocellulose-coated side of the bottom slides.
Close the top with clean top slides to complete the flow cell assembly.
Seal the flow cells by placing them on a heater plate set to 80-100 °C for approximately 1 minute.
Prepare TE tethering buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 1 mM EDTA, and 200 mM NaCl).
Alternatively, prepare PBS+ buffer (137 mM NaCl, 2.7 mM KCl, 10 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.4) supplemented with 100 μg/ml BSA, 0.1% Tween, and 5 mM sodium azide.
Flush 2-3 cell volumes TE tethering buffer into the flow cell.
Incubate 0.5 or 1.5 μm radius non-magnetic latex beads in the flow cell for ~30 min.
Rinse out unattached non-magnetic beads by flushing with 2-3 cell volumes of TE tethering buffer.
Functionalize the bottom surface of the flow cell by incubating it with 100 μg/ml anti-digoxigenin in PBS for at least 1 hr (preferably overnight).
Rinse the flow cell with 2-3 cell volumes of TE tethering buffer.
Incubate the flow cell with 2 mg/ml bovine serum albumin (BSA) in TE tethering buffer for 30 min for surface passivation.
Take an aliquot of 2 ml streptavidin-coated superparamagnetic MyOne beads.
Dilute the beads with 10 ml TE tethering buffer.
Wash the beads twice with 10 ml TE tethering buffer using a magnetic particle concentrator.
Resuspend the beads in 10 ml TE tethering buffer.
Incubate ~1 ml of DNA molecules (approximately 1 ng) with the beads for 30 min in TE tethering buffer.
Dilute the solution of DNA-tethered superparamagnetic beads ten-fold by adding 90 μl TE tethering buffer.
Inject the diluted solution into the flow cell.
Incubate the solution in the flow cell for ~1 hr to allow DNA attachment to the anti-digoxigenin-coated surface.
Wash the flow cell thoroughly with TE tethering buffer.
Flush extensively with experimental buffer to remove all non-attached beads.
For measurements requiring fiducial marker beads, incubate the flow cell with a 1,000-fold diluted stock of marker beads in TE tethering buffer for at least 30 min.
Rinse the flow cell thoroughly with buffer after incubation.
Search for rotationally constrained DNA molecules in the flow cell using a conventional MT with appropriate field configuration and both translational and rotational control of the magnet position.
Apply pulling forces of ≥ 1 pN to distinguish tethered beads from beads stuck to the surface by their different heights in the focus.
Introduce 20-30 turns of the magnets at a force of ≈ 0.25 pN to assess whether a DNA molecule is rotationally constrained.
Verify that the bead is attached by a single DNA tether by comparing behavior under positive and negative turns at forces of > 1 pN.
Search for appropriate fixed beads stuck to the bottom surface in the vicinity of the tether of interest to serve as reference beads.
Calibrate the length of the DNA, l.
Bring the tethered bead in contact with the surface by rotating the magnet approximately 60 turns at a force below 0.2 pN.
Measure the vertical position of the tethered bead relative to the flowcell surface.
Record a rotation curve at a stretching force of ≈ 0.25 pN.
Determine the number of turns at which the extension is maximal, indicating torsional relaxation.
Fit the rotation curve locally with a parabolic or Gaussian function to determine the center position.
Define this point as “zero turns”.
For a series of approximately 20 magnet positions, determine the average extension of the torsionally-relaxed molecule from the z-trace.
Manually replace the square magnets of the conventional magnetic tweezers by a cylindrical magnet for FOMT.
Ensure the selected DNA tether remains within the field of view during the replacement process.
Unscrew the complete magnet head that holds the magnets for the conventional tweezers configuration.
Replace it with a magnet head that holds a cylindrical magnet for FOMT.
Record the (x,y) excursions of a magnetic bead tethered by a single dsDNA tether.
Determine the corresponding location within the characteristic fluctuation pattern using recorded data.
Perform coarse alignment of the cylindrical magnet above the flow-cell using (x,y) translation stages.
Move the cylindrical magnet in the appropriate direction if the (x,y) excursions follow an arc.
Complete coarse alignment when measurement of the (x,y) excursions results in circular motion.
Perform fine alignment in the FOMT using high-resolution micrometer screws or an automated stage.
Position the magnet or flow cell to center the cylindrical magnet onto the bead within ~10 µm.
Adjust the position such that fluctuations on the circle annulus are nearly uniform, corresponding to a kBT energy barrier.
Calibrate the force in the FOMT if required for analysis.
Use either the bead’s radial fluctuations <r2> or local field gradient for calibration.
Measure DNA torque using magnetic torque tweezers.
Replace the cylindrical magnet with a cylindrical magnet plus a side magnet for MTT.
Ensure the selected DNA tether remains within the field of view during replacement.
Manually add the side magnet at its proper location within 1 minute.
Track angular fluctuations as a function of time θ(t) using fiducial based tracking protocol or (x,y)-position monitoring.
Record full images of the bead as a function of time for subsequent image processing if using fiducial based tracking protocol.
Record the bead’s (x,y) fluctuations at this step if using angular tracking protocol based on monitoring (x,y)-position.
Rotate magnets slowly (typically at 0.1 Hz) by several turns for recording time trace.
Convert Cartesian coordinates (x,y) into polar coordinates (r,θ).
Determine the stiffness of the torsional trap from the variance of angular fluctuations using kθ = kBT / σθ2.
Record the z-position of the bead and use this to determine tether length l.
Rotate N turns.
Record θ(t) and l(t).
Determine the torque accumulated in the nucleic acid tether after N turns using: Γ = − kθ <θN - θ0>.
Repeat steps as necessary to fully determine a molecule’s torque response in a single measurement run.
